desc:
A rooted tree whose children are ordered but where every node may have any number of children (not just two) has distinct node values. You are given its preorder (a node, then each of its child subtrees from first to last) and its postorder (each child subtree from first to last, then the node) traversal. Unlike for binary trees, where a lone child can be left or right, these two traversals determine such a tree uniquely.

Return the parent of every node as an array parents of the same length: parents[i] is the value of the parent of preorder[i], and -1 for the root.

For preorder = [1, 2, 3, 4] and postorder = [3, 2, 4, 1] the tree is: 1 has the children 2 and 4, and 2 has the child 3. The answer is [-1, 1, 2, 1]. For preorder = [1, 2, 3] and postorder = [2, 3, 1] the root has two children, so the answer is [-1, 1, 1]; with postorder = [3, 2, 1] it is a chain and the answer is [-1, 1, 2].
constraints: postorder is a permutation of preorder, and both come from the same ordered rooted tree
hints: Node x is an ancestor of node y exactly when x comes before y in preorder and after y in postorder.
Walk through the preorder array and keep the path of ancestors that are still "open" on a stack. Which nodes on the stack are not ancestors of the new node?
A node t on top of the stack is finished (not an ancestor of the next node x) when t appears before x in postorder. Pop such nodes; the node left on top is the parent of x. Then push x.
editorial: In a tree, x is a proper ancestor of y exactly when x is visited before y in preorder (we enter x first) and after y in postorder (we leave x last). The parent of y is the deepest ancestor, i.e. the ancestor that is entered latest.

Process the nodes in preorder and keep the stack of the current root-to-node path. For the next node x, a stack node t is no longer an ancestor if t was already left before x was left, that is, if its postorder index is smaller than that of x. Such nodes are popped from the top; the first node that survives is the parent of x (the stack is ordered from the root down, and ancestry is nested). Every node is pushed and popped at most once, so the algorithm is linear with a value-to-postorder-index map.

For binary trees the same traversals are ambiguous only because a lone child could be a left or a right child; here the tree has no such left/right distinction, so the parent array is the whole answer.
